SFN-21 Build Super Console as the modular self-hosted administration control plane

## Executive summary Build **Super Console**, the modular self-hosted administration control plane for the Superfunctions ecosystem. A deployment explicitly registers the Superfunctions it uses, and the console exposes only those enabled product modules across navigation, UI routes, REST/OpenAPI, TypeScript admin clients, and MCP. ## Problem Superfunctions currently expose uneven operator surfaces: CiFn has a standalone React dashboard, CmsFn has an early Studio shell, WatchFn has a placeholder dashboard, AuthFn has limited admin routes, and most functions have no coherent administration UI or stable admin API. Consumers need one composable operator experience without conflating operator administration with customer-facing portals. ## Desired outcome A production-quality, self-hosted Super Console built at `superconsole/` with SvelteKit, Tailwind, and UIFn. Each function owns an admin capability manifest and service contract; the console mounts selected modules, shared administration APIs, TypeScript clients, OpenAPI descriptions, and McpFn-backed tools. The universal tenancy model is organization/workspace → project → environment. ## Scope ### Shared platform * SvelteKit console shell powered by UIFn; repair UIFn at source when gaps or defects are found. Workarounds and parallel visual systems are prohibited. * Explicit deploy-time module registration and capability discovery. Disabled modules must not appear or remain addressable through UI, REST, OpenAPI, or MCP. * AuthFn-powered operator identity, sessions, tenancy, RBAC, and service authentication. * Audited mutations and shared audit-event contracts; use the relevant Superfunction for each platform concern rather than duplicating substitute implementations. * Versioned language-neutral REST API and generated OpenAPI. * TypeScript admin SDK generated or composed from stable contracts. * McpFn-backed discoverable admin tools, including scoped and audited mutations. * Shared organization/workspace, project, environment, module, navigation, search, notification, usage, and error primitives. * Port the existing CiFn dashboard behavior into the shell. ### Required product modules AuthFn, BillFn, BrowseFn, CiFn, CmsFn, CompFn, DataFn, FileFn, FlowFn, HostFn, MailFn, MemoryFn, PlugFn, RecFn, SearchFn, SecFn, SendFn, TestFn, UserFn, and WatchFn. CatchFn and LogFn are owned by WatchFn modules. ContentFn is owned by CmsFn. ### Optional product modules ApiFn, BotFn, CacheFn, DocsFn, LangFn, and ProbeFn. They use the same capability contract and are enabled only when configured. ## Hard architecture rules 1. UIFn is the sole shared visual system for the operator console. 2. Customer-facing portals remain distinct from operator administration. 3. Every product module consumes its function-owned admin service/capability contract; the console may compose but must not redefine domain logic. 4. Relevant Superfunctions power console concerns—for example AuthFn for identity/RBAC, McpFn for MCP exposure, WatchFn/LogFn/CatchFn for observability, SecFn for security controls, and FileFn for managed artifacts. 5. Admin REST paths are versioned, described by OpenAPI, and consumable independently of the console. 6. The TypeScript admin SDK and MCP tools preserve the same authorization, scope, validation, error, pagination, idempotency, and audit semantics as REST. 7. Disabled modules are absent from every exposure surface. 8. Existing non-admin SDK compatibility is preserved; breaking changes are allowed only in unfinished admin APIs where necessary. ## Non-goals * A hosted Superfunctions cloud control plane. * Python admin SDKs in this delivery. * Standalone admin applications for ChartFn, CliFn, DrawFn, ExtFn, IconFn, LogFn, McpFn, or UIFn. * A separate ContentFn console. * Merging end-customer portals into operator administration. * Pushing a branch or opening a pull request as part of this local implementation. ## Acceptance criteria * `superconsole/` provides a working self-hosted SvelteKit console shell, configuration model, tenancy selector, module registry, RBAC guards, navigation, routing, error states, and audit visibility. * All 21 required and 6 optional modules are implemented through real capability manifests and usable operator views; CatchFn/LogFn are nested in WatchFn and ContentFn is nested in CmsFn. * CiFn dashboard capabilities are ported to the shell rather than embedded as a second application. * Only explicitly enabled modules appear or respond through UI, REST/OpenAPI, TypeScript SDK, and MCP. * Function-owned administration contracts cover their operator objects and mutations, with consistent validation, pagination, errors, idempotency, authorization, and audit metadata. * OpenAPI and TypeScript admin SDK surfaces are generated/verified and usable without the console. * McpFn exposes equivalent scoped tools; mutations are authorization-checked and audited. * UIFn source changes cover every shared UI need discovered during implementation, with no one-off visual-system bypasses. * Local architecture, capability inventory, rules, API/MCP model, security/tenancy model, module rollout, testing, operations, and decision records live under `superconsole/.conduct/SFN-/` after issue creation. * Automated tests cover registry filtering, authorization, tenancy isolation, route/API/MCP exposure, audit emission, representative module behavior, and the migrated CiFn workflows. * Build, typecheck, lint, unit, integration, and relevant UI checks pass. * Work is kept local in an isolated exact-head worktree with coherent separate commits and no push/PR. ## Dependencies UIFn, AuthFn, McpFn, WatchFn, LogFn, CatchFn, SecFn, DataFn, FileFn, the shared HTTP/database packages, and function-specific domain services. Existing CiFn dashboard behavior is the migration source. ## Risks and mitigations * **Uneven function maturity:** define a strict common capability contract and implement real domain-adapter boundaries rather than placeholder pages. * **Authorization drift across surfaces:** one policy decision and request context must govern UI, REST, SDK, and MCP. * **Accidental module exposure:** derive all routes, schemas, tools, and navigation from the validated deployment registry. * **UI inconsistency:** enforce UIFn imports and fix missing primitives in UIFn itself. * **Cross-tenant leakage:** require explicit tenant/project/environment scope and isolation tests for every request. * **Large delivery surface:** use parallel non-overlapping implementation tracks, contract tests, and coherent local commits. ## Open questions No product decisions are blocking implementation. Low-level implementation details will be recorded as architecture decisions and validated against the current repository during delivery. ## Supporting documents * [Ideation & Product Rationale — SFN-21]() * [Architecture & Delivery Plan — SFN-21]()

### Socket protects your app from malicious dependencies lurking in your open source supply chain.

Open source code makes up 90% of most codebases. It is critical to manage it effectively to reduce your security risk.

## Detect and block open source supply chain attacks

Security teams depend on Socket to prevent malicious open source dependencies from infiltrating their apps.

Socket dramatically improves your open source security posture by _detecting and blocking the attacks you don't expect_ – malware, install scripts, hidden code, typo-squatting, and more – which aren't caught by traditional vulnerability scanners.

- **Block malware** – Block emerging malware threats

- **Block typo-squatting** – Block malicious packages that differ in name by only a few characters, and recommend the correct package

- **Detect hidden code** – Detect obfuscated, minified, or hidden code

- **Detect privileged API usage** – Report when a dependency update introduces new risky API usage – filesystem, network, child_process, eval()

- **Detect suspicious updates** – Sudden inclusion of privileged APIs in patch or minor releases

Socket currently [supports 80+ detections](https://socket.dev/alerts) in 5 categories: supply chain risk, quality, maintenance, known vulnerabilities, and license problems.

## Take charge of your dependency health

Socket improves security outcomes and reduces work for security teams by **surfacing actionable security information directly inline in GitHub** so developers are empowered to make better decisions.

- **Five minute deployment** – The easiest security product you'll ever deploy in your organization. Just install a GitHub app and you're done.

- **Provide security feedback directly on PRs** – Empower developers to solve security issues before they're deployed into production.

- **Automated security** – Spend security team resources auditing the highest-impact dependencies, instead of all or nothing.

## Socket detects what vulnerability scanners can’t

It's no longer sufficient to scan for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and stop there. And yet, that's what the leading "supply chain security" products do, leaving you vulnerable.

It can take weeks or months for a CVE to be discovered, reported, and detected by tools. But in today's culture of fast development, a malicious dependency can be updated, merged, and running in production in days or even sometimes hours.

Defenders need a new approach to address emerging threats from malicious dependencies:

- **Maintainer intentionally added malware** – Rogue maintainer sabotaged his own open source package with 100M downloads/month, affecting companies such as Amazon AWS

- **Package hijacked and poisoned w/ cryptominers and password-stealing malware** – Deliberate malware introduced into multiple packages with 30M downloads/month each

- **Package hijacked to add backdoor targeting a specific organization** – Obfuscated malware added to a dependency which targeted a single company, went undetected for over a week, and made it into their production build

- **NPM package manager allowed anyone to publish new versions of any package** – Attackers could publish new versions of any NPM package without authorization _for multiple years_

Using third-party dependencies without proper vetting leaves you open to hacking, breaches, and assorted security misfortune.

Prompt for AI agents (unresolved issues) ```text Check if these issues are valid — if so, understand the root cause of each and fix them. If appropriate, use sub-agents to investigate and fix each issue separately. P1: A workspace-scoped operator can enqueue reconciliation for another tenant by supplying its `billingAccountId` or `subscriptionId`, because `reconcileProvider` ignores the active context. Resolve and validate reconciliation targets against the active scope before enqueueing the job. P2: A typo or unsupported provider is accepted and persisted as a reconciliation job because this cast performs no runtime validation. Reject unsupported provider names before calling `enqueueReconciliationJob`, preferably with the supported-provider enum in the input schema. P1: When an operator has selected a non-default scope, clicking `Inspect` drops all scope query parameters. The run detail request then falls back to the principal's default scope, which can show the wrong run data or make a valid run inaccessible. Preserve the current scope when building this destination, using the same `scopedConsoleHref(..., page.url.searchParams)` pattern as `ResourceTable`. P1: When `options.server.calendarRuntime.enabled` is true, every admin operation starts a new calendar polling interval and discards its handle. Disable `calendarRuntime` for this per-request router to prevent unbounded polling and duplicate scheduling. P1: For a get-only resource, `resource.apiHref` contains an unmaterialized `:id`; list requests send it literally, while detail requests append the identity after it. Keep separate collection/detail hrefs and omit collection pages when no list operation exists. P1: When `datafn.records.list` paginates, this passes the admin cursor string directly to DataFn, which expects an `{ after | before }` cursor object; it also drops DataFn's object `nextCursor`. Decode the admin cursor before querying and re-encode the returned DataFn cursor for the admin API. P1: When an inline pipeline run is listed or opened through the admin dispatcher, the output fails schema validation because CiFn represents it with empty repository and ref values. Use a separate output schema that permits the inline sentinel while keeping non-empty values required for trigger input. P2: Inline pipeline definitions can place credentials under arbitrary keys, but the required trigger audit records `pipelineSpec` without field-level redaction. Redact the entire `pipelineSpec` input in the operation metadata or reject embedded secret material before auditing. P1: Triggering a run starts repository-defined jobs that can produce external effects, but `cifn.runs.trigger-run` executes without confirmation. Require explicit high-risk confirmation, as `cifn.runs.retry-run` does. P2: When an operator uses ArrowDown and Enter, the command controller changes its selection but never calls `choose`, so keyboard command execution does nothing. Handle `onValueChange` on `CommandRoot` and route the selected command through `choose`. P1: Typing a command's visible label hides every result because UIFn filters `CommandItem` values (`overview`, `search`, or `module-*`), while this component filters the rendered labels. Use a label/group searchable value (or otherwise provide the item's text value) so the UIFn filter and `filtered` agree. P2: When the API returns a signed external `downloadHref`, this handler rejects it because `openSafeAdminDownload` defaults `signedExternal` to false. Return the signed-external flag from the loader and pass it when opening the download. P2: When a job has more than 1,000 log lines, this view permanently hides lines after the first page and Follow logs keeps reloading that same page. Add pagination, and use a tail or cursor strategy while following. P2: When any scope identifier contains `/`, `MemoryUserFnOperatorStore` aliases distinct scopes because `key` joins components without escaping. Encode the complete scope tuple before using it as the map key. P2: When the module overview request returns 401, 404, 405, or 5xx, this branch falls through to normal content and silently shows partial or stale registry data. Handle every `data.loadError`, using `forbidden` only for 403 and `error` otherwise, before rendering the module content. P2: The generic Super Console cannot render the `stats` resource because its collection operation returns `item` instead of `items`. Return a list-shaped result with a stable statistics row, or model this resource as a singleton detail operation. P2: When a namespace contains more than 100 keys, `cachefn.keys.list` silently hides the remainder while claiming there is no next page. Add cursor pagination and a matching `pagination` definition, or stop truncating the response. P2: When the bound cache uses IndexedDB, `cachefn.stats.list` fails response validation because `getStats()` includes `memoryUsage: undefined`. Omit undefined optional fields before returning the stats object. P2: When an operator searches from a later page, `search()` retains the old `cursor` parameter. The backend applies that cursor to the new `q`, so results can start mid-list or fail; delete `cursor` before navigating. P2: When a caller uses the supported legacy `googleMaps` alias or surrounding whitespace, this looks up rate-limit state under the wrong key and returns a noncanonical provider ID. Normalize and trim the provider, or reject aliases, before calling `getRateLimitStatus` and constructing `item`. P2: When the registry request fails with a non-401/403 error while overview succeeds, this falls through and reports “No modules enabled” from the empty fallback registry. Render an error state for `data.shell.error` before rendering registry-dependent content. P2: Mutating a nested metadata property on an inserted input or search result changes the stored memory. Deep-clone JSON metadata when storing and returning records. P2: Nested or array metadata filters return no results in the memory adapter because `Object.is` compares references, not JSON values or containment. Implement recursive JSONB-compatible containment matching. P2: Inserting a duplicate memory ID silently overwrites the existing record and still reports both inputs as saved. Reject duplicate IDs before mutating the map to match the Postgres primary-key contract. P2: Without a threshold, mismatched-dimension embeddings are returned as low-quality results because `-Infinity` is sorted but not excluded. Filter invalid similarities before applying `topK`. P2: When the CiFn list operation returns cursor pagination, the cursor is serialized in `result.page`, not `result.data`. Read `result.page?.nextCursor` as a fallback so the Next page control remains available. P2: The log download path can never produce a download with the current CiFn admin contract. Add the URL fields and a download-capable adapter to the output schema, or remove this UI path. P2: When `config.basePath` ends with `/`, every delegated AuthFn route gets a doubled slash and sign-in, 2FA completion, and sign-out return 404. Normalize the configured base path or join it with route paths before forwarding requests. P2: After sign-out, the persistent root layout keeps this receipt visible on `/sign-in` and for the next operator in the same tab. Clear `mutationFeedback` at logout and when entering an unauthenticated session. P2: When two action buttons overlap, an older `invalidateAll()` can finish after a newer mutation and publish last, so the shell displays the older receipt. Add a generation check or serialize refresh publication so stale completions cannot overwrite the latest operation. P2: When a class-based `BrowseFnAdminService` uses `this` in a method, this adapter invokes the extracted method without its receiver, causing the operation to throw or read the wrong state. Preserve the service receiver for every mapped method, or wrap each call as `(...args) => service.listProviders(...args)`. P2: When an object or array field contains invalid nested values, `validateActionInput` accepts it and dispatches the action, which then fails server-side. Recursively validate parsed values against `field.schema`, including `items` and nested `properties`, before returning them. P2: The compatibility router now drops OpenAPI metadata from every admin route, so OpenAPI generation silently omits the legacy admin surface. Restore the auth and OpenAPI metadata on all three routes, or explicitly migrate this router’s documented OpenAPI integration. P2: When clients send `?limit=`, `parseOptionalInt` converts the blank value to `0`, and user listing returns a 400 instead of using the default limit. Treat trimmed blank values as `undefined` before calling `Number(value)`. P2: A cursor from one FileFn collection can be reused for another collection in the same scope because the cursor carries only an offset.
